41	\subsection{Schema Confusability Score (SCS)}
42	\label{sec:scs}
43	
44	\looseness=-1
45	We define the Schema Confusability Score (SCS) to quantify semantic overlap between types in a schema. Given a type $t$ with name string $\text{name}(t)$, an embedding function $\text{embed}(\cdot)$ maps the type name to a vector representation. The \textbf{pairwise SCS} between types $t_i$ and $t_j$ is:
46	{\small
47	\[
48	\text{SCS}(t_i, t_j) = \cos\bigl(\text{embed}(\text{name}(t_i)),\; \text{embed}(\text{name}(t_j))\bigr)
49	\]
50	}
51	
52	For a batch of types $B = \{t_1, \ldots, t_k\}$, the \textbf{Batch Confusability Score (BCS)} aggregates all pairwise similarities:
53	\[
54	\text{BCS}(B) = \frac{1}{\binom{k}{2}} \sum_{i < j,\; t_i, t_j \in B} \text{SCS}(t_i, t_j)
55	\]
56	
57	We use two embeddings to provide complementary perspectives: Qwen3 captures the extraction model's own type representations (self-similarity), while MiniLM provides an independent general-purpose baseline. Cross-embedding consistency holds on all datasets (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_bcs_sensitivity}); MiniLM consistently yields equal or stronger correlations, which confirms that Qwen3-based estimates are conservative. We compute SCS with: (1)~Qwen3-32B \citep{qwen3-2025} hidden-state representations (5{,}120-d) and (2)~all-MiniLM-L6-v2 \citep{minilm-2020,sentence-bert-2019}, a 384-d sentence encoder. Few-NERD uses Qwen3 because its fine-grained same-category pairs (e.g., ``person-artist'' vs.\ ``person-actor'') require the higher-dimensional space. MiniLM is the primary BCS embedding because sentence-transformers are trained for semantic similarity \citep{sentence-bert-2019}; Qwen3 causal-LM states show compressed BCS range (std${}\,=\,0.034$ vs.\ MiniLM std${}\,=\,0.081$), consistent with autoregressive anisotropy \citep{ethayarajh-contextual-2019}. Name-only SCS yields equivalent predictive accuracy to name+definition ($\Delta r$: $-0.023$ to $+0.035$; Appendix~\ref{app:scs-ablation}).

tool_args.old_string: Figure~\ref{fig:main_results}a shows RE accuracy declines monotonically with schema size (0.86$\to$0.50 for FewRel). NER recall declines through intermediate counts (0.51$\to$0.27, plateauing across counts 22--44) before partial recovery at full-schema (0.41), where eliminating type-filtering overhead restores extraction performance. DocRED replicates the monotonic RE pattern (88.0\%$\to$38.7\%, $-$56\%; Appendix). MAVEN exhibits a reversed trend attributable to centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}). The effect replicates on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($-$43\,pp on Few-NERD; per-batch $r = 0.725$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}). The pattern is stable across three seeds (max $\Delta = 10.7$\,pp, within 1\,SD; intra-batch variance exceeds inter-seed variance by ${>}$5$\times$; Appendix~\ref{app:variance-decomposition}). Formal trend analysis confirms monotonic RE decline (Jonckheere-Terpstra $J = 109{,}707$, $p < 0.001$). Count decline replicates on LLaMA-70B with comparable magnitude and on Gemini Flash (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_cross_model_gemini}). Count curves establish trend direction; magnitude estimation relies on the higher-powered BCS-controlled experiments (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
tool_args.new_string: Figure~\ref{fig:main_results}a shows RE accuracy declines monotonically with schema size (0.86$\to$0.50 for FewRel). NER shows a U-shaped pattern (0.51$\to$0.27$\to$0.41), with partial recovery at full-schema where type-filtering overhead is eliminated. DocRED replicates the monotonic RE pattern (88.0\%$\to$38.7\%, $-$56\%; Appendix). MAVEN exhibits a reversed trend attributable to centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}). The effect replicates on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($-$43\,pp on Few-NERD; per-batch $r = 0.725$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), is stable across seeds (Appendix~\ref{app:variance-decomposition}; Jonckheere-Terpstra $p < 0.001$), and extends to LLaMA-70B and Gemini Flash (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_cross_model_gemini}). Count curves establish trend direction; magnitude estimation relies on the higher-powered BCS-controlled experiments (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).

tool_args.old_string: Direct regression on 100 random 16-type batches from the 80-relation pool yields a conservative restricted-range estimate: $r = -0.22$, $R^2 \approx 0.05$, $p = 0.027$, with BCS explaining ${\sim}$5\% of cross-batch accuracy variance (80-pool BCS SD${}\,=\,0.044$ vs.\ pooled SD${}\,=\,0.141$). The pooled analysis across count levels and pool sizes (semipartial $R^2 = 0.273$, $n = 204$; \S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}) provides the primary variance estimate. DocRED pooled $R^2 = 0.578$ ($n = 110$) is inflated by multicollinearity (VIF${}\,=\,50.9$; semipartial $R^2_{\text{BCS}} = 0.056$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_partial_corr}). The typical BCS span (IQR = 0.054) yields an expected accuracy gap of 2.2\,pp (95\% CI [0.4, 4.0]). Quartile comparison confirms: bottom-quartile BCS batches average 82.8\% vs.\ 78.9\% for top-quartile ($\Delta = 3.9$\,pp). The amplification from pairwise $r^2 \approx 1.5\%$ to pooled semipartial $R^2 \approx 27.3\%$ is not a statistical artifact but the operative mechanism. Correlated confusable-type interactions compound within shared prompts \citep{robinson-1950-ecological,baan-2023-ecological}, producing the batch-level signal that makes BCS practically predictive (${\sim}3\times$ amplification illustrated by Monte Carlo simulation; Appendix~\ref{app:aggregation-sim}).
tool_args.new_string: Direct regression on 100 random 16-type batches within the 80-relation pool yields a conservative restricted-range estimate ($r = -0.22$, $R^2 \approx 0.05$, $p = 0.027$) due to narrow BCS range (SD${}\,=\,0.044$ vs.\ pooled SD${}\,=\,0.141$). The pooled analysis (semipartial $R^2 = 0.273$, $n = 204$; \S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}) provides the primary variance estimate; DocRED pooled $R^2 = 0.578$ ($n = 110$) is inflated by multicollinearity (VIF${}\,=\,50.9$; semipartial $R^2_{\text{BCS}} = 0.056$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_partial_corr}). Quartile comparison: bottom-BCS batches average 82.8\% vs.\ 78.9\% for top-BCS ($\Delta = 3.9$\,pp; IQR-based expected gap: 2.2\,pp, 95\% CI [0.4, 4.0]). The amplification from pairwise $r^2 \approx 1.5\%$ to pooled semipartial $R^2 \approx 27.3\%$ reflects the operative mechanism: correlated confusable-type interactions compound within shared prompts \citep{robinson-1950-ecological,baan-2023-ecological}, producing the batch-level signal (${\sim}3\times$ amplification; Monte Carlo simulation in Appendix~\ref{app:aggregation-sim}).

tool_args.old_string: These results establish two dimensions: \textbf{Dimension~1} (count predicts recall decline) and \textbf{Dimension~2} (confusability predicts type confusion). The full-range regression ($n = 69$, five count levels) serves as the primary separability test; the $2 \times 2$ factorial ($n = 54$) as a sensitivity check. We select the equivalence margin via convergent evidence: (i)~an interaction exceeding the main effect magnitude would undermine dimensional separability; (ii)~Cohen's $d = 0.5$ \citep{cohen-1988-statistical} (medium effect) at the within-cell SD of 4.6\,pp yields $\pm 2.3$\,pp. Both converge on $\pm 2\text{--}3$\,pp.\footnote{Margin sensitivity (Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity}) confirms equivalence from $\pm 2$\,pp ($p = 0.047$) through $\pm 5$\,pp.} On the linear scale, TOST \citep{lakens-2017-equivalence,schuirmann-1987-tost} bounds the FewRel interaction within $\pm 3$\,pp ($p = 0.003$); at $\pm 2$\,pp, equivalence is marginal ($p = 0.047$). Probability-scale TOST is the primary analysis because accuracy values (0.37--0.86) remain in the mid-range where logit and linear scales yield similar inference. The logit-scale result is inconclusive ($p = 0.209$; regression-based TOST: $p = 0.050$ at $\pm 3$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}). On DocRED, the raw factorial interaction ($-$9.4\,pp) is confounded by narrower BCS ranges at count 32; range-matched analysis reduces it to 0.93\,pp, consistent with bounded interaction (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}). In NER, batch-level BCS signal is not detected at current power (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}). Two factors explain the asymmetry: (1)~NER errors distribute across miss, boundary, and type modes rather than concentrating in type substitution (relaxed matching confirms this is not a metric artifact; Appendix~\ref{app:relaxed-matching}), and (2)~BCS range restriction (SD ratio 19\%) limits statistical detection power to 65\% (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ner_power}). The factorial test is inconclusive ($p = 0.50$). At $n{=}450$ with BCS SD${}\,=\,0.027$, the minimum detectable correlation is $|r| \approx 0.132$ ($\alpha = 0.05$, power${}\,=\,0.80$), while FewRel's $r = -0.57$ would attenuate to $r \approx -0.11$ under this SD compression. Current evidence cannot distinguish absence of a BCS$\to$NER effect from an effect too small to detect---absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Post-hoc mitigation attempts---type renaming to reduce SCS and few-shot prompting---fail to close the confusability gap (Appendices~\ref{app:renaming},~\ref{sec:appendix_fewshot_bcs}), confirming that BCS captures a structural property of the schema--model interaction rather than a surface-level naming artifact.

The equivalence margin ($\pm 2\text{--}3$\,pp) is calibrated from main-effect magnitude and Cohen's $d = 0.5$ \citep{cohen-1988-statistical}.\footnote{Margin sensitivity (Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity}) confirms equivalence from $\pm 2$\,pp ($p = 0.047$) through $\pm 5$\,pp.} On the linear scale, TOST \citep{lakens-2017-equivalence,schuirmann-1987-tost} bounds the FewRel interaction within $\pm 3$\,pp ($p = 0.003$); the logit-scale result is inconclusive ($p = 0.209$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}). On DocRED, the raw interaction ($-$9.4\,pp) reduces to 0.93\,pp after range matching (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}). In NER, batch-level BCS signal is not detected: errors distribute across miss, boundary, and type modes rather than concentrating in type substitution (Appendix~\ref{app:relaxed-matching}), and BCS range restriction (SD ratio 19\%) limits detection power to 65\% (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ner_power}). The factorial test is inconclusive ($p = 0.50$); current evidence cannot distinguish absence of a BCS$\to$NER effect from an effect too small to detect. Post-hoc mitigation---type renaming and few-shot prompting---fails to close the confusability gap (Appendices~\ref{app:renaming},~\ref{sec:appendix_fewshot_bcs}), confirming that BCS captures a structural property of the schema--model interaction.
